clue.text: Is out of incidents producing poems

definitions.note: plural, matching the plural answer: lyric poems of a classical form

indicators.note: 'Is out of' tells us those two letters leave the word for the incidents

parts.note: episodes are incidents or happenings
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is missing from a series of happenings, and the result is verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' removes IS from EPISODES, leaving the classical lyric form.
explanation.definitionFit: An epode is a type of lyric poem in which a long line is followed by a shorter one, as in Horace.

clue.text: Explanatory words before attentive audience?

parts.note: pre is a prefix meaning before
an attentive audience presents rows of watching faces

explanation.surface: Opening remarks given to a listening crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attentive audience' pictures listeners, but here it is what a speaker sees: rows of upturned faces.
explanation.definitionFit: Introductory remarks at the start of a book explain its purpose or scope.

clue.text: Cornel in autumn: by Constable

explanation.surface: A dogwood in its autumn colours as painted by Constable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable' looks like the painter, but it is the comic constable of Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The cornel or dogwood bears this fruit in autumn, and Shakespeare's bumbling watchman in Much Ado About Nothing has the same name.

clue.text: Street rag preceded by horse got strung out

annotationWithheld.clue: Street rag preceded by horse got strung out

clue.text: Blind envy of the French

explanation.surface: A sightless person's jealousy of France.
explanation.definitionFit: A slatted window shutter is a blind of this name, and the French word for jealousy is spelt the same way.

clue.text: Mechanic named to raise the whole nation out of the red ?

definitions.text: Mechanic named to raise the whole nation out of the red

parts.words: Mechanic named to raise the whole nation out of the red
parts.note: a jack is a lifting device, and lifting all trades out of debt would save the economy; the phrase names a handyman

explanation.surface: A worker appointed to rescue the country's economy from debt.
explanation.walkthrough: A jack raises things, so a jack 'of all trades' would raise every trade into profit; the phrase means a handyman, an old sense of mechanic.
explanation.definitionFit: A handyman who can turn his hand to any job; 'mechanic' once meant any manual worker.

clue.text: Fury at dismissal ? Shocking affair

parts.note: a batsman given out has been dismissed in cricket
rage is fury or great anger

explanation.surface: A batsman is furious at being given out, a scandalous business.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket: a dismissed batsman is out. 'Fury at dismissal' reads as one angry batsman; 'at' only sets the two pieces beside each other.
explanation.definitionFit: A scandal or atrocity provokes great public anger and indignation.

clue.text: Pets turn on another — nothing but a way of playing

indicators.note: turn means the word for pets is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: cats are common household pets
another pet of the same kind, one more cat
nothing is zero, the letter o

explanation.surface: Pets turn on each other, and there is nothing to it but a style of play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' makes STAC from CATS; 'another' is one more cat, then O for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, playing each note short and detached is a style of performance.

clue.text: One of the realms travelled by Keats?

definitions.text: One of the realms travelled by Keats?

parts.words: One of the realms travelled by Keats?
parts.note: Keats's sonnet on Chapman's Homer opens 'Much have I travell'd in the realms of gold'

explanation.surface: Asking which places the poet Keats visited.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's line 'Much have I travell'd in the realms of gold' points to the legendary city of gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary city of gold sought by Spanish explorers in South America is a realm of gold.

clue.text: Place of one of the nosy

definitions.text: Place of one of the nosy

parts.words: Place of one of the nosy
parts.note: a French town that gave its name to a famous long-nosed swordsman-poet of Rostand's play

explanation.surface: Asking where a busybody comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nosy' reads as inquisitive, but it means big-nosed: Cyrano, of Rostand's play, took his name from this town in the Dordogne.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyrano de Bergerac, famed for his enormous nose, is named after this town in south-west France.

clue.text: A London yarn, by the way

explanation.surface: A tall story told in the capital, mentioned in passing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the way' points to the London sense being a road: the Strand is a famous street in central London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Strand is a well-known thoroughfare in central London, and a strand is a single thread or fibre of yarn.

clue.text: A short Greek novel translated into Romany

definitions.note: a noun for the language, describing the Romany word that titles the book

indicators.note: translated means the words are turned into another form, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: Gr. is the short form, or abbreviation, of Greek
taken as written

explanation.surface: A brief Greek work of fiction is rendered into the Gypsy tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translated' rearranges A, GR and NOVEL. George Borrow's 1851 novel takes its title from a Romany word meaning 'word-master'.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of George Borrow's novel is a Romany word, meaning a master of words or philologist.

clue.text: Red can perhaps' excel on points

definitions.note: a verb phrase describing what the answer, a noun, does: a ballerina excels on the tips of her toes

indicators.note: perhaps suggests these letters could be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A tin of something red might shine on the scoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges RED CAN. 'On points' is ballet, dancing on the tips of the toes, not scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballet performer may shine when dancing on pointe, on the tips of the toes.

clue.text: Placed on one's trusty steed, for instance

definitions.text: Placed on one's trusty steed, for instance

parts.words: Placed on one's trusty steed, for instance
parts.note: the trust or confidence a rider puts in a dependable horse

explanation.surface: Someone sits astride a faithful horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Placed on' reads as mounting the horse, but it is the trust one places on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dependence or trust is what one places on something one can count on, such as a faithful horse.

clue.text: Missile systems at full stretch

parts.note: devices that hurl stones by stretching an elastic band or arm, read as weapons systems

explanation.surface: Defence weapons stretched to their limits.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests military forces under strain; the devices here launch missiles by being stretched taut.
explanation.definitionFit: A forked stick with elastic, or a siege engine, throws a stone when its band or arm is drawn back tight.

clue.text: Tossed hay's all burnt up

indicators.note: hay that is tossed is thrown about, so its letters are mixed up

parts.note: the word hay with its S

explanation.surface: Hay pitched in the field has been destroyed by fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tossed' rearranges HAYS, using the S of the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wholly burnt is reduced to cinders and grey powder, like the residue of a fire.

clue.text: Put them in an anti-aircraft envelope, curse it!

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: an envelope wraps around its contents, so the anti-aircraft letters enclose them

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An exasperated order to put the items into an envelope, with a swear word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'envelope' wraps the anti-aircraft letters round THEM. 'Curse it!' reads as an exclamation, but the definition is the noun 'curse'.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal ban or denunciation by the Church, and more broadly a detested thing, is a curse.

clue.text: Beautiful youth goes to pot if confined to the house

definitions.text: goes to pot if confined to the house

explanation.surface: A handsome young man goes to seed if kept indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Hyacinthus was a lovely youth loved by Apollo; the flower named after him is often grown in pots indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: The spring bulb is named after Apollo's beloved Hyacinthus, and is commonly forced in pots indoors.

clue.text: Such a lot of water a locomotive holds

indicators.note: holds says the answer is contained within the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Asking how much water a steam engine's tank can carry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' points to the letters inside 'a locomotive'. 'Lot' hides 'lake': this is the Italian lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Como in northern Italy is a large body of water.

clue.text: No end of a bike, so be it — but not for Daisy

definitions.note: a flower, but not the daisy

indicators.note: no end of means the last letter of the bike word is dropped

parts.note: a cycle is a bike
amen means so be it

explanation.surface: Someone bids farewell to a bicycle's end, but it isn't Daisy's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' cuts E from CYCLE. Daisy, of the song, had 'a bicycle made for two'; here the flower is a cyclamen, not a daisy.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyclamen is a flowering plant, a bloom other than the daisy.

clue.text: Brilliant, like the weather?

explanation.surface: Praising how dazzling the climate is.
explanation.walkthrough: Meteorology is the study of weather, so the second sense plays on that word.
explanation.definitionFit: A dazzling rise is like a shooting star, and the adjective once meant relating to the atmosphere and its weather.

clue.text: I'd look back with an effort to a heathen practice

parts.note: I'd minus its apostrophe

indicators.note: looking back means the word for look is written backwards

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
an gives the letter a
a try is an attempt or effort

explanation.surface: Someone looks back on a struggle that led to pagan worship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LO into OL. LO is an archaic word meaning 'look!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Worshipping images or false gods is the practice the Bible condemns among heathens.

clue.text: Send to Coventry one 'thus deceased

definitions.note: a British idiom for refusing to speak to someone

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
so means thus
late means dead or deceased

explanation.surface: Someone is shunned once they are dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send to Coventry' is a British idiom meaning to ostracise someone, not a trip to the Midlands city.
explanation.definitionFit: To ostracise someone is to cut them off from the group's company.

clue.text: Unacceptable face from old Japan ?

parts.note: Edward Heath's phrase 'the unacceptable face of capitalism', applied to a business magnate, whose title comes from a Japanese word for a shogun

explanation.surface: Asking about a disgraced figure from Japanese history.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Heath, a British prime minister, called a company's conduct 'the unacceptable face of capitalism'; the word for a capitalist magnate comes from Japanese taikun, 'great lord', a title of the shogun.
explanation.definitionFit: A business magnate is the face of capitalism, and the word came from a Japanese title for the shogun.

clue.text: Parchment in an old pen was off-putting

definitions.note: past tense, matching the answer: drove away or disgusted

indicators.note: in tells us the parchment goes inside the old pen

parts.note: a reed was cut and used as a pen in ancient times
pell is an old word for a skin or parchment roll

explanation.surface: A scroll found in an ancient pen put people off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the parchment inside the old pen. A pell is an old word for a skin or roll of parchment, as in the Exchequer's Pell Office.
explanation.definitionFit: To have driven away or disgusted someone is to have been off-putting to them.

clue.text: Any notice, say, of the Nine'?

indicators.note: say signals the words are spoken, so we want what they sound like

parts.note: any plus ad, a notice or advertisement, spoken together

explanation.surface: Asking whether the Muses had any announcement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' tells us to hear 'any ad', a notice being an advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: A group or set of nine, as the nine Muses are often called the Nine.

clue.text: Poet bilingually akin to Newbolt ?

parts.note: a poet whose surname, read in French then Latin, means 'of the sea', like Henry Newbolt, writer of sea poems

explanation.surface: Comparing two English poets across languages.
explanation.walkthrough: French 'de la' (of the) plus Latin 'mare' (sea) give 'of the sea', the subject of Newbolt's naval poems such as 'Drake's Drum'.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter de la Mare was an English poet whose surname reads in two languages as 'of the sea'.

clue.text: Let heats be' arranged for them

definitions.text: Let heats be' arranged for them

indicators.note: arranged means set out in a new order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Organisers set up the qualifying races for the competitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' rearranges LET HEATS, and the whole clue describes who runs in heats.
explanation.definitionFit: Sports competitors run in qualifying races, which are set up for them.

clue.text: Eroded isthmus in the main for: a' Roman 'philosopher.

indicators.note: in tells us the worn-down strip of land sits inside the main

parts.note: the main is a literary name for the sea

indicators.note: eroded means worn away, here the last letter is worn off

parts.note: a neck is a narrow strip of land, an isthmus

explanation.surface: A narrow land bridge worn away in the ocean, for an ancient thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eroded' wears K off NECK to give NEC, which goes 'in' SEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a Stoic philosopher and tutor to the emperor Nero.
